1. Two workload roles allow every S3 and every Bedrock action on all resources 1 · Decide firstDays of workCost neutralPlatform/DevOps setting

The ECS task role shared by catalog-api and order-api allows s3:* on *, and the chatbot instance role allows bedrock:* on *. The S3 permission covers every bucket in the account, including the CloudTrail bucket and the images bucket that also stores the chatbot code artifact and Kubernetes manifests. No service-specific scoping exists in the templates.

Why it matters A fault or compromise in one container reaches far beyond what it needs: it could delete account-wide data or replace the chatbot code that the next instance boot installs. The Bedrock permission includes creating models, agents and provisioned throughput, which carry cost. The protections already in place are private subnets only, no public endpoints, GuardDuty on and CloudTrail on.

Suggestion Narrowing the shared ECS task role to s3:GetObject on the images bucket prefix the catalog uses, and giving catalog-api and order-api one task role each, would contain a fault in one service. This can be done after confirming in the code that order-api does not read S3. For the chatbot, InvokeModel and InvokeModelWithResponseStream on the two model ARNs it calls, with a guardrail condition, would replace bedrock:*. Moving the chatbot artifact and k8s manifests to a dedicated artifact bucket that only the pipeline writes would close the code-replacement path.

References
  • SEC03-BP02 Grant least privilege access
  • Security best practices in IAM
  • IAM Access Analyzer policy generation
  • Security best practices in IAM

2. Every component connects to the database with the master credential, and data-tier traffic is not encrypted 2 · Plan nextWeeks of workCost neutralApplication change needed

Three roles (ECS task role, EKS RecommendationRole, chatbot instance role) can read the Aurora master secret shopnow/db, which has never been rotated. Aurora PostgreSQL 16 with the default parameter group does not require TLS (rds.force_ssl=0). Redis runs without in-transit encryption or AUTH. The Aurora and Redis security groups admit the whole app CIDR 10.70.10.0/23, including the bastion and every EKS pod.

Why it matters A compromise of any one service, or of any pod in the cluster, reaches the whole database with full administrative rights, and cache traffic can be read on the network path. Storage encryption at rest is already on for Aurora, Redis and the EBS volumes.

Suggestion One database role per service in its own rotated secret, with the master secret kept for administration, would limit each service to its own tables. A custom cluster parameter group with rds.force_ssl=1 and sslmode=verify-full in the clients would make TLS mandatory. Turning on TransitEncryption (preferred mode first, then required) with an AUTH token on replication group shcdhz1twytdux5 would do the same for Redis. Replacing the 10.70.10.0/23 rules in DbSg and CacheSg with the clients' security groups would close the remaining paths. The changes can be staged per service so the application keeps working.

References
  • SEC09-BP02 Enforce encryption in transit
  • ElastiCache in-transit encryption (TLS)
  • Authenticating with the AUTH command (ElastiCache)
  • SEC02-BP05 Audit and rotate credentials periodically
  • Rotate AWS Secrets Manager secrets

3. Database, cache and chatbot each run as a single instance in one Availability Zone 2 · Plan nextList price +$213/moDays of workCost upPlatform/DevOps setting

The Aurora cluster has one writer (db.r6g.large, us-east-1b) and no reader, with 1-day backup retention, deletion protection off and DeletionPolicy Delete in the template. Redis is one cache.t4g.small node in us-east-1b with no snapshots. The chatbot is one t3.large in us-east-1a with no Auto Scaling group. No AWS Backup plan covers any of them. The ECS services and the ALBs, by contrast, already span both AZs.

Why it matters A failure of the writer, the Redis node or us-east-1b stops catalog-api, order-api and recommendation together, and the chatbot stops with us-east-1a. Deleting the shopnow-data stack would remove the database with no final snapshot. In this non-production testbed that means lost test data and a rebuild. Before customer traffic it becomes an outage.

Suggestion Turning on DeletionProtection, setting DeletionPolicy to Snapshot and raising BackupRetentionPeriod to at least 7 days are template changes with almost no cost and protect against the largest loss. Adding an Aurora reader in us-east-1a and a Redis replica with Multi-AZ failover would remove the single-AZ dependency. If cost decides it for the testbed, an Aurora Serverless v2 reader or keeping a single Redis node as a documented disposable cache are smaller steps. The chatbot could move into a container service behind the existing internal ALB.

List prices net +$213/month (AWS Price List API, On-Demand; not a bill forecast)

4. No alerting path is configured in the AWS account, and most tiers emit no alarms or control-plane logs 1 · Decide firstDays of workCost upPlatform/DevOps setting

The only alarm (catalog CPU) publishes to SNS topic shopnow-alerts, which has no subscriptions. There are no alarms on the ALBs, Aurora, Redis, EKS, order-api or the EC2 instances. EKS control-plane logging, Container Insights, the EKS observability add-on and Bedrock model invocation logging are all off. The dashboard's ALB widget points to a placeholder load balancer. The order-api log group has had no events since the deployment on 2026-11-06. Whether an external tool covers any of this is not visible.

Why it matters A failure in any tier would not trigger an alert from AWS, and the evidence needed to explain it afterwards (API audit, request logs, model prompts and responses) is not recorded.

Suggestion Subscribing the on-call channel to shopnow-alerts and sending a test message is a setting change that makes the existing alarm useful. A small alarm set per tier would follow: ALB 5XX and UnHealthyHostCount, Aurora CPU and connections, ECS running task count, EC2 status checks. Together with EKS control-plane logging (api, audit, authenticator), Container Insights and Bedrock invocation logging with log retention set, failures would become visible and explainable. If an external monitoring tool is already in use, the same signals can be routed there instead.

5. Three of four services have no deployment pipeline in this account, and the one pipeline has no test or rollback gate 2 · Plan nextWeeks of workCost neutralPlatform/DevOps setting

Only catalog-api has CodeCommit → CodeBuild → ECS deploy. order-api, storefront and recommendation exist only as single `latest` images pushed on 2026-11-06, and order-api's task definition runs `:latest` from a mutable repository. The catalog pipeline builds and deploys with no test, image scan or approval step. ECS deployment circuit breakers are off, and ECR scan-on-push and Inspector are disabled.

Why it matters A broken image reaches the running services without a check, there is no automatic rollback, and for three services there is no recorded version to return to.

Suggestion Turning on the ECS deployment circuit breaker with rollback for both services, and tag immutability with scan-on-push on the four repositories, would add a safety net at almost no cost. Extending the catalog pipeline pattern to the other three services, with a unit-test step, an image scan gate and commit-SHA tags, would make every change traceable and reversible. Where their source lives today is the first question for the owner.

6. The non-production environment runs fixed, previous-generation capacity around the clock 3 · LaterExample, before measurement: −$442/moWeeks of workMeasure firstPlatform/DevOps setting

The EKS node group is fixed at 2 × m5.2xlarge On-Demand (x86) for two small services, Aurora is a provisioned db.r6g.large, and two NAT gateways, two ALBs, a t3.large and four Fargate tasks run 24/7. No scaling, schedule, Spot or Graviton is used. Pod requests and utilisation were not measured, so the oversizing is inferred.

Why it matters The testbed pays production-sized list prices for capacity that is probably idle much of the time, and the account bill already grows month over month (other projects drive most of it).

Suggestion Measuring the storefront and recommendation pod requests first would show how much node capacity they need. Smaller Graviton nodes, Spot for non-production, or EKS Auto Mode / Karpenter would then follow; the m7g.large pair is only an example size. Aurora Serverless v2 with a low minimum, a single NAT gateway for the testbed and scheduled scale-down outside working hours are further options, and a consistent CostCenter tag would make the workload's own cost visible.

Current architecture

Evidence: 461 successful read-only queries, collection status partial, 541 resources in us-east-1. Host internals, database contents, traffic and cost were not collected.

Support plan. The Trusted Advisor and Health APIs answered "subscription required", which points to the Basic or Developer plan for this account (the owner question below asks for the actual plan), so this report contains no Trusted Advisor checks or Health notices of planned changes and end-of-support dates. The AWS Health Dashboard in the console still shows those notices on every plan; only the API needs Business or higher.

Compliance obligations. The scope interview did not name any. If the workload handles personal or health data, or falls under rules such as ISMS-P or PCI DSS, the services below that keep continuous evidence (Security Hub standards, the Config recorder, Inspector, IAM Access Analyzer) move from optional to worth enabling, and whether the data may stay in us-east-1 is worth confirming.

Services worth considering

Each service below is off or only partly on. None of them is required: whether it earns its place depends on the workload's requirements, compliance obligations and the tooling the team already runs. The notes say what the service does, what turning it on would add here, and when leaving it off is a reasonable choice.

Security Hub Not enabledConsider

What it is AWS Security Hub collects findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, IAM Access Analyzer, Config and partner tools into one view and evaluates the account continuously against security standards such as the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices, CIS or PCI DSS.

What enabling adds One place to see and triage control failures across accounts and regions, a score per standard, and automation rules that route or suppress findings. Standards need the AWS Config recorder.

For this workload Worth considering when several teams share the account or a compliance standard (CIS, PCI DSS, NIST) has to be shown: Security Hub would bring the GuardDuty findings already produced here into one place and run this report's one-time checks (load balancer TLS, ECR, EKS and Secrets Manager controls) continuously. A single team that reviews GuardDuty findings directly can defer it; it can be enabled later without any change to the workload.

Finding f0092 · Documentation

AWS Config recorder Not enabledConsider

What it is AWS Config records the configuration of resources over time and evaluates managed or custom rules against that history.

What enabling adds A timeline of what changed and when, drift detection against templates, compliance views, and the data Security Hub standards rely on. Priced per configuration item recorded and per rule evaluation.

For this workload AWS Config keeps a timeline of each resource's configuration, evaluates rules against it and supplies the data Security Hub standards read. It matters most where resources change outside CloudFormation. 73% of the tagged resources here carry CloudFormation stack tags; the other 27% were created outside CloudFormation (by hand or by another tool). If the team works from stack templates with drift detection and the account is small, the recorder can wait; if an audit trail of changes or Security Hub standards are wanted, consider recording the resource types this workload uses (Config is priced per configuration item, so recording every type in a busy account adds cost).

Finding f0094 · Documentation

Amazon Inspector Not enabledConsider

What it is Amazon Inspector scans EC2 instances (through the SSM agent), container images in Amazon ECR and Lambda functions for known software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure.

What enabling adds A prioritised list of packages to patch with a risk score, rescanned automatically when new CVEs are published. Priced per instance, image and function scanned.

For this workload Amazon Inspector scans EC2 instances (through the SSM agent), container images in ECR and Lambda function packages for known vulnerabilities (CVEs) and lists the packages to patch in priority order. This workload has 4 EC2 instances and 4 ECR repositories that it would cover. If images are already scanned in the CI pipeline or by another scanner and instances are patched on a schedule, Inspector may add little; otherwise the ECR and EC2 scans are a low-effort way to see where patching is needed.

Finding f0095 · Documentation

IAM Access Analyzer Not enabledConsider

What it is IAM Access Analyzer reports resources whose policies grant access from outside the account or organization (S3 buckets, IAM roles, KMS keys, SQS queues, Secrets Manager secrets, RDS snapshots and more) and can validate policies and find unused access.

What enabling adds A list of externally reachable resources the team can confirm or close; external-access analysis is free.

For this workload IAM Access Analyzer lists S3 buckets, IAM roles, KMS keys, SQS queues, Secrets Manager secrets and other resources that principals outside the account can reach, so intended sharing can be confirmed and the rest closed. An external-access analyzer is free and one per region is enough. For this workload it would review its 2 S3 buckets and 1 secret and the roles they trust; worth creating in any account that shares data with other companies or other accounts.

  • sg-0example00001 Configuration: the Aurora security group allows 5432 from 10.70.10.0/23 (both app subnets). Every host there can reach the Aurora endpoint: the chatbot, the kubectl bastion, both EKS nodes and every pod, and the ECS tasks. Only some of them use it. m0014
  • sg-0example00002 Configuration: the Redis security group allows 6379 from 10.70.10.0/23 (both app subnets). Every host there can reach the Redis endpoint: the chatbot, the kubectl bastion, both EKS nodes and every pod, and the ECS tasks. Only some of them use it. m0015

What to do Replace the CIDR rule with source security groups of the actual clients (ECS TaskSg, EKS pod security group or node SG, ChatbotSg).

Findings m0014, m0015 · Evidence e0115, s0011 · Sources docs.aws.amazon.com
m0016 · Aurora TLS not required AURORA_TLS_NOT_REQUIREDWarn · WARNseverity MediumAPI configuration

Target shopnow-data-dbcluster-example00001

What we saw Configuration: the cluster uses default.aurora-postgresql16, where rds.force_ssl defaults to 0 for Aurora PostgreSQL 16 and older (AWS docs, read 2026-11-15). The server therefore accepts unencrypted connections. Source: catalog-api does not set sslmode, so libpq's default 'prefer' applies, and a client or proxy can downgrade the connection.

What to do Use a custom cluster parameter group with rds.force_ssl=1 and set sslmode=verify-full with the RDS CA bundle in every client. Plan for this anyway: the default flips to 1 at a major upgrade to 17.

m0017 · EKS admin long term user EKS_ADMIN_LONG_TERM_USERWarn · WARNseverity MediumAPI configuration

Target EKS access entry for one IAM user with long-term keys (cluster shopnow)

What we saw Configuration: one IAM user with long-term access keys has an EKS access entry with AmazonEKSClusterAdminPolicy at cluster scope (AdminPrincipalArn parameter). Stage 1 recorded that this user has long-term access keys and broad write rights, and the account summary shows no root MFA. The bastion role is also cluster-admin.

What to do Map cluster-admin to an IAM Identity Center permission set or role assumed with MFA, scope the bastion to the namespaces it deploys, and remove the user entry.

CheckSeverityHow firmlyResourceRecommendation
IAM wildcard permissionHighStrongly recommended
  • role/shopnow-ecs-TaskRole-LYfwFb04VAfs · app
  • role/shopnow-genai-InstanceRole-VR63Qdfh4abE · chatbot
Replace service-wide wildcards with the actions the workload calls and the specific resource ARNs; generate a starting policy from CloudTrail with IAM Access Analyzer.
EKS control plane loggingMediumRecommended
  • shopnow

Elasticache transit encryptionMediumRecommended
  • replicationgroup:shcdhz1twytdux5
Enable in-transit encryption (preferred, then required mode) and AUTH or RBAC users; update clients to TLS.
DB shared master credentialMediumRecommended
  • secret:shopnow/db-eMZxND
Create one database role per service with only the grants it needs, store each in its own secret with rotation (Secrets Manager managed rotation or RDS-managed master password), and keep the master secret for administrators only.
Root MFAHighStrongly recommended
  • Root user
Confirm with the organization's administrators whether centralized root access manages this account. If it does not, enable MFA on the root user (a hardware key or passkey), store it where two people can reach it, and stop using root for daily work.

  • loadbalancer/app/shopnow-internal/0example00000001
  • loadbalancer/app/shopnow-eks-ingress/0example00000002

ECR tag immutabilityMediumRecommended

Secret rotationMediumRecommended

Securityhub enabledMediumRecommended
  • Security Hub · us-east-1
Worth considering when several teams share the account or a compliance standard (CIS, PCI DSS, NIST) has to be shown: Security Hub would bring the GuardDuty findings already produced here into one place and run this report's one-time checks (load balancer TLS, ECR, EKS and Secrets Manager controls) continuously. A single team that reviews GuardDuty findings directly can defer it; it can be enabled later without any change to the workload.
Inspector enabledMediumRecommended
  • Amazon Inspector · us-east-1
Amazon Inspector scans EC2 instances (through the SSM agent), container images in ECR and Lambda function packages for known vulnerabilities (CVEs) and lists the packages to patch in priority order. This workload has 4 EC2 instances and 4 ECR repositories that it would cover. If images are already scanned in the CI pipeline or by another scanner and instances are patched on a schedule, Inspector may add little; otherwise the ECR and EC2 scans are a low-effort way to see where patching is needed.
IAM access analyzerMediumRecommended
  • IAM Access Analyzer · us-east-1
IAM Access Analyzer lists S3 buckets, IAM roles, KMS keys, SQS queues, Secrets Manager secrets and other resources that principals outside the account can reach, so intended sharing can be confirmed and the rest closed. An external-access analyzer is free and one per region is enough. For this workload it would review its 2 S3 buckets and 1 secret and the roles they trust; worth creating in any account that shares data with other companies or other accounts.
VPC flow logsMediumRecommended
  • vpc-0example00001
Enable VPC Flow Logs (rejected traffic at least) to CloudWatch Logs or S3 with a retention rule.
Data tier SG scopeMediumRecommended
  • sg-0example00001
  • sg-0example00002
Replace the CIDR rule with source security groups of the actual clients (ECS TaskSg, EKS pod security group or node SG, ChatbotSg).
Aurora TLS not requiredMediumRecommended
  • shopnow-data-dbcluster-example00001
Use a custom cluster parameter group with rds.force_ssl=1 and set sslmode=verify-full with the RDS CA bundle in every client. Plan for this anyway: the default flips to 1 at a major upgrade to 17.
EKS admin long term userMediumRecommended
  • EKS access entry for one IAM user with long-term keys (cluster shopnow)
Map cluster-admin to an IAM Identity Center permission set or role assumed with MFA, scope the bastion to the namespaces it deploys, and remove the user entry.
Artifact in data bucketMediumRecommended
  • shopnow-data-example00003-vxnr68dwirnv
Move build and deploy artifacts to a dedicated, versioned artifact bucket that only the pipeline can write, and verify a checksum before install.
ELB drop invalid headersLowOptional

Set the attribute to true (Security Hub ELB.4) after checking that no client depends on invalid headers.

S3 endpoint policyLowOptional

Specialist SA Agent recommendations

5 Specialist SA Agents (Container & Serverless Specialist SA Agent, Database Specialist SA Agent, Data Analytics Specialist SA Agent, GenAI Specialist SA Agent, DevOps Specialist SA Agent), AI agents that each take the role of an AWS specialist solutions architect, reviewed this workload's evidence in their area. Each says what they see, what they would change and why, what they would leave for now, and draws the change. The combined target architecture follows.

Container & Serverless Specialist SA Agent ConditionalNot recommendedConditional

shopnow runs four small services on three runtime platforms: catalog-api and order-api on ECS Fargate, storefront and recommendation on an EKS cluster with a fixed two-node m5.2xlarge node group and a kubectl bastion, and the chatbot on one t3.large EC2 instance in us-east-1a. The first thing I would raise is the chatbot, the only user-facing component with a single copy and no automatic replacement. After that, the ECS services would benefit from scaling and a health check that reflects their dependencies, and the team could consider whether EKS earns its operating cost for two services.

What we see now

  • catalog-api and order-api run on ECS Fargate (task size 512 CPU units, 1024 MiB, X86_64), two tasks each, spread across us-east-1a and us-east-1b behind the internal ALB shopnow-internal. This part already works the way a small service should: no servers to patch and one task per AZ. e0071 e0072 s0113 s0031 s0032 catalog-api order-api
  • Both ECS services have a fixed desiredCount of 2 and no Application Auto Scaling target. catalog-api's ALB health check (/catalog/health) returns ok without touching Aurora or Redis, so a task that has lost its database stays in service. f0070 f0071 m0024 s0033 s0133
  • The EKS cluster shopnow (Kubernetes 1.35, private endpoint only) runs storefront and, by its Pod Identity association, recommendation on node group shopnow-default, fixed at min/desired/max 2/2/2 m5.2xlarge On-Demand, plus a t3.small bastion for kubectl. Standard support for 1.35 ends on 2027-03-27. The Deployments, requests/limits and autoscaling of those pods could not be read. m0012 f0120 m0030 s0114 s0005 shopnow
  • The chatbot is one t3.large instance in us-east-1a with no Auto Scaling group or load balancer; UserData installs it from a tarball in S3 with pip and a systemd unit, so there is no recorded version on the instance and no way to roll back to a previous build. m0020 m0021 s0020 i-0example00002
  • Both internal ALBs listen on HTTP:80 only and keep invalid header fields. The catalog-api image is built from python:3.12-slim with no USER line, so the process runs as root in the container. f0038 f0039 f0040 f0042 s0132
  • The source and templates show only synchronous HTTP calls. The one EventBridge rule starts the CI/CD pipeline on a push, and the SNS topic shopnow-alerts carries alarms; neither is part of the application's request path. s0133 s0077 shopnow-cicd-OnPush-4Riv8x4mK9yG shopnow-alerts

Not now

  • Moving catalog-api, order-api or the chatbot to Lambda. They are working synchronous HTTP services, and catalog-api opens a new database connection on every request with no pool, which counts against a per-invocation model. I would revisit this if an event-driven unit (a file upload, a scheduled job, a queue consumer) appears. m0025 s0133 catalog-api
  • Adding SQS, SNS, EventBridge or MSK to the application. The evidence shows no asynchronous step or coupling problem; the existing rule and topic serve CI/CD and alarms. What would decide it: is any step allowed to finish after the user gets a response (order confirmation, email, recommendation refresh), and does a slow dependency today block a request it should not? s0133 s0077 shopnow-cicd-OnPush-4Riv8x4mK9yG shopnow-alerts
  • Graviton (ARM64) for the Fargate tasks or nodes. The images are built for X86_64 and no utilisation was measured. Worth considering after the platform decision above, once the build produces multi-arch images. f0075 s0134
  • Splitting services further, a service mesh or a rewrite. Nothing in the evidence asks for it; four services behind two ALBs is a structure the team can keep. s0008 s0005

Recommendations

1. Give the chatbot a second copy and automatic replacement by running it as an ECS Fargate service Example, before measurement: −$61/moWeeks of workMeasure first

What changes Package the chatbot (the contents of chatbot.tgz and its requirements.txt) as a container image in a new ECR repository, with a non-root USER and an image tag per build. Run it as an ECS Fargate service in cluster shopnow with desiredCount 2 in subnets shopnow-app-a and shopnow-app-b, behind a new target group on port 8000 with the existing /health path, reached through a path rule on shopnow-internal. Give the task its own task role carrying the permissions the instance role holds today. Once traffic has moved, retire instance i-0example00002 and the Chatbot resource in shopnow-genai.

What it gives An instance or AZ failure no longer removes the chatbot: ECS replaces a failed task and the second task keeps answering. Each release becomes a tagged image, so a bad build can be rolled back by pointing the service at the previous tag, and the chatbot joins the platform and pipeline pattern the team already runs for catalog-api.

List prices net −$61/month (an example at published On-Demand rates for one possible configuration; the size is decided after measurement, so the figure is not a saving or a cost to plan on)

Check whether the chatbot keeps any local state (files, in-memory sessions) that two copies would need to share. Measure CPU and memory of the current instance to size the Fargate task instead of copying t3.large.

Alternatives Keep EC2: move the UserData into a launch template and run an Auto Scaling group of two instances across us-east-1a and us-east-1b behind a target group on shopnow-internal (price ct-p006). This fixes availability but keeps the tarball deployment. Keep the single instance and only add an EC2 auto-recovery alarm, accepting an outage during an AZ event.

How to undo Keep the EC2 instance running until the ECS service has served traffic; to undo, remove the path rule so shopnow-internal no longer forwards to the new target group, point clients back at the instance on port 8000 and delete the service.

2. Let catalog-api and order-api scale with load and leave service when their database is unreachable Days of workMeasure first

What changes Register both services with Application Auto Scaling (minimum 2, a maximum agreed with the owner) and add a target-tracking policy on ECSServiceAverageCPUUtilization. Add a readiness endpoint to catalog-api that runs a short query against Aurora with a timeout and point target group shopnow-catalog at it, keeping /catalog/health as a liveness check; check whether /orders/health on order-api does the same and align it.

What it gives Capacity follows demand instead of staying at two tasks, and the ALB stops sending requests to a task that cannot reach Aurora, so ECS replaces it.

Before deciding Turn on Container Insights first (handed to DevOps) and look at CPU, memory and request patterns to pick the target value and maximum. Decide what a failed dependency should do: Redis is optional in the code (errors are ignored), Aurora is not, so only Aurora belongs in the readiness check. Agree the maximum with the Database Specialist SA Agent, because every extra task opens its own connections (m0025).

Alternatives Keep the fixed count of two and add a scheduled scaling action for known peaks only. Keep the shallow health check and rely on alarms on 5XX responses to detect a task that has lost the database.

How to undo Deregister the scalable targets (the services keep their current desiredCount) and point the target group health check back at /catalog/health.

4. Serve the internal ALBs over HTTPS and drop invalid headers Days of workCost up

What changes Add an HTTPS:443 listener with an ACM certificate and the ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-2021-06 policy to shopnow-internal and shopnow-eks-ingress, change HTTP:80 to a redirect, set routing.http.drop_invalid_header_fields.enabled=true on both, and open 443 in their security groups.

What it gives Traffic between clients in the VPC and the services is encrypted, and requests with malformed headers are dropped at the load balancer instead of reaching the application.

Before deciding Which clients call these ALBs today, and can they trust a private certificate (AWS Private CA) or do they need a public certificate for an internal name? Do any clients send headers with invalid characters that would now be dropped?

Alternatives Keep HTTP inside the VPC and document the decision, relying on the security groups that limit callers to the VPC CIDR, while the account remains non-production.

How to undo Remove the redirect so HTTP:80 forwards again, set drop_invalid_header_fields back to false and delete the HTTPS listener.

Database Specialist SA Agent Conditional

The shopnow data tier is an Aurora PostgreSQL 16.13 cluster with a single db.r6g.large writer in us-east-1b and a single-node Redis cache in the same zone, both encrypted at rest. Recovery guards are thin (one day of backups, no deletion protection, DeletionPolicy: Delete, no AWS Backup plan), every workload role reads the master credential, and neither Aurora nor Redis requires TLS. The Database Specialist SA Agent would raise the free recovery settings first, then separate and encrypt database access, and only then add paid failover targets once the owner states recovery goals for this non-production environment.

What we see now

  • Aurora cluster shopnow-data-dbcluster-example00001 (aurora-postgresql 16.13, standard support until 2029-02-28) has one writer, shopnow-data-dbwriter-example00002, in us-east-1b and no reader. Aurora keeps six copies of the storage across zones, so the data survives a zone loss, but a writer failure stops reads and writes until a new instance is created. m0005 e0026 e0007 s0049
  • Automated backup retention is 1 day, DeletionProtection is off, the shopnow-data stack sets DeletionPolicy and UpdateReplacePolicy to Delete on the cluster, and the account has no AWS Backup plan. No restore or failover test is recorded. m0007 m0008 f0073 f0129 s0011 s0051 s0054
  • The secret shopnow/db holds the Aurora master user and has never been rotated. The shared ECS task role, the EKS RecommendationRole and the chatbot instance role can all read it, and catalog-api connects with it, so every component has superuser rights. m0013 f0067 s0053 s0133
  • The cluster uses default.aurora-postgresql16, where rds.force_ssl is 0, and catalog-api does not set sslmode; the server accepts unencrypted connections. Storage is encrypted with KMS, and the database security group admits only the app subnets 10.70.10.0/23. m0016 e0026 s0011
  • Redis replication group shcdhz1twytdux5 (cache.t4g.small, one node in us-east-1b) has no transit encryption, no AUTH, no replica, no automatic failover and no snapshots. In the catalog-api source it holds product lists with a 60-second expiry and the service falls back to the database on a cache error; the description also names sessions, which the evidence does not show. m0004 m0009 m0023 e0220 s0052 s0133
  • catalog-api opens a new psycopg connection for every request without a pool, and Performance Insights and Enhanced Monitoring are off, so there is no utilisation data for sizing. m0025 s0133 e0007

Not now

  • Moving to another engine such as DynamoDB or a different relational engine: the evidence shows relational queries on PostgreSQL (and the stack describes pgvector use), and nothing shows the current engine failing. s0011 s0133
  • Changing the writer class from db.r6g.large: Performance Insights and Enhanced Monitoring are off, so there is no utilisation data. Sizing is measure_first; turning on Database Insights would give the data. e0007 m0031
  • Aurora Serverless v2 or stopping the cluster outside working hours for this non-production environment: worth considering for cost once the owner confirms usage hours and the writer's load has been measured; the containers and DevOps reviews own the other always-on resources. m0031
  • A major version upgrade to Aurora PostgreSQL 17: 16 is in standard support until 2029-02-28. Note that rds.force_ssl defaults to 1 from 17, so the TLS change above also prepares the upgrade. s0049 m0016
  • Aurora Global Database or cross-Region backup copies: the scope states no multi-Region requirement. e0026

Recommendations

1. Turn on the free recovery guards for the Aurora cluster Setting changeCost neutral

What changes In the shopnow-data template, set DeletionProtection: true, BackupRetentionPeriod to the agreed recovery window (7 days is a common starting point for a testbed), and DeletionPolicy and UpdateReplacePolicy: Snapshot on DbCluster. Then add an AWS Backup plan that selects the cluster and keeps copies in a separate vault with its own retention, and run one restore of a point-in-time copy into a new cluster to record how long it takes.

What it gives A logical error or a bad deployment can be undone from point-in-time recovery for the whole window instead of one day; a stack deletion or replacement keeps a final snapshot; a deletion by mistake is refused; the restore test turns an unknown recovery time into a recorded one.

Before deciding Agree the recovery point objective (RPO, how much data may be lost) and recovery time objective (RTO, how long the service may be down) with the owner. Backup storage up to the size of the cluster volume is included; check the volume size before choosing a long retention or long AWS Backup copies.

Alternatives Keep the current settings and document that the environment can be rebuilt from scratch with seed data, if the owner confirms nothing in it needs to be recovered. Raise retention and turn on deletion protection only, without an AWS Backup plan, when one recovery path is enough.

How to undo Restore the previous template values (retention 1, DeletionProtection false, DeletionPolicy Delete) and delete the AWS Backup plan; existing snapshots stay until their retention ends. No data moves and the writer keeps all writes.

Based on m0007 m0008 f0073 f0129 shopnow-data-dbcluster-example00001

2. Give each service its own database user and require encrypted connections Weeks of workCost up

What changes Create one PostgreSQL role per consumer (catalog-api, order-api, the recommendation service and the chatbot) with only the grants it needs, store each in its own Secrets Manager secret with managed rotation, and keep shopnow/db for administrators only (or switch the master to an RDS-managed master password). Attach a custom cluster parameter group with rds.force_ssl=1 and set sslmode=verify-full with the RDS CA bundle in every client. For Redis shcdhz1twytdux5, enable in-transit encryption (preferred mode first, then required) with an AUTH token or RBAC users, and update clients to TLS.

What it gives A compromised component reaches only its own tables instead of the whole database; rotation limits the life of a leaked password; Aurora and Redis no longer accept plain-text connections from the app subnets.

Before deciding List which tables each service reads and writes; the source for order-api, the recommendation service and the chatbot was not part of the evidence. Confirm every client library supports TLS and re-reads its secret after rotation (catalog-api caches the secret in memory until the task restarts). Changing rds.force_ssl is applied at a reboot of the writer; plan a short write interruption. Each additional secret carries a small monthly charge.

Alternatives IAM database authentication for the services, which removes stored passwords but adds a token refresh in each client. Keep the shared credential but turn on rotation and require TLS as a first step, when per-service roles cannot be scheduled yet.

How to undo Point a service back at shopnow/db and drop its role; attach default.aurora-postgresql16 again and reboot to accept non-TLS clients; for Redis, set transit encryption back to preferred. The writer stays the only write authority throughout, so no data has to be reconciled.

Based on m0013 f0067 m0016 m0004 db-eMZxND shopnow-data-dbcluster-example00001 shcdhz1twytdux5

What changes Add an Aurora reader in us-east-1a (subnet shopnow-db-a) to cluster shopnow-data-dbcluster-example00001 with promotion tier 0, and run a failover test. If sessions must survive a node loss, add a Redis replica in us-east-1a to shcdhz1twytdux5 with Multi-AZ, automatic failover and daily snapshots; if Redis holds only rebuildable catalog entries, document it as a disposable cache instead.

What it gives A writer or zone failure promotes the reader behind the same cluster endpoint instead of stopping catalog-api, order-api, the recommendation service and the chatbot; the cache primary endpoint moves to the replica without a client change.

List prices net +$213/month (AWS Price List API, On-Demand; not a bill forecast)
  • + $190/month · Aurora reader db.r6g.large in us-east-1a (1 x Aurora PostgreSQL db.r6g.large, On-Demand, us-east-1; storage, I/O, backups beyond the free allowance and data transfer excluded; 730 hours a month; p001)
  • + $23/month · Redis replica cache.t4g.small (1 x Redis cache.t4g.small node, On-Demand, us-east-1; data transfer and backups excluded; 730 hours a month; p002)

Before deciding The scope marks this environment as non-production: decide whether it has to show production availability or only reproduce production's design. Ask what Redis holds beyond the catalog entries seen in catalog-api, and whether a lost session is acceptable. Confirm the clients use the cluster endpoint, not the instance endpoint.

How to undo Delete the reader and the Redis replica and restore the template values; the writer and the Redis primary keep all writes, so nothing has to be reconciled.

Based on m0005 m0009 m0023 shopnow-data-dbcluster-example00001 shcdhz1twytdux5

4. Pool database connections in catalog-api before considering RDS Proxy Days of workCost neutral

What changes Replace the per-request psycopg.connect in catalog-api db_conn() with a psycopg_pool ConnectionPool opened at start-up, sized per task so that two tasks stay well below max_connections of the writer, and apply the same pattern to the other services once their source is reviewed.

What it gives Requests stop paying for a new TCP, TLS and authentication handshake, and a traffic burst cannot exhaust the writer's connection limit through catalog-api alone.

Before deciding Turn on Performance Insights (Database Insights) to see the connection count and wait events before and after the change. Check how order-api, the recommendation service and the chatbot open connections.

Alternatives RDS Proxy in front of the cluster, when several services share the database and a failover should keep client connections; it also allows IAM authentication at the proxy and is billed per vCPU of the writer. Keep per-request connections at the current traffic level, if measurement shows connection setup is not a problem.

How to undo Redeploy the previous catalog-api image; the database is unchanged.

Before deciding: create a custom aurora-postgresql16 cluster parameter group with rds.logical_replication=1 and aurora.enhanced_logical_replication=1 (enhanced logical replication writes all column values to the WAL and could raise write I/O on the single writer), reboot the writer to apply it, confirm every replicated table has a primary key and the database uses UTF-8, and agree a data filter that leaves out personal columns that reports do not need. Redshift cost depends on query volume and would need measuring first. m0016 m0005 shopnow-data-dbwriter-example00002
  • If a daily or weekly view is enough, an Aurora DB cluster export to S3 (Parquet, from a clone, so the live cluster is not loaded) queried with Amazon Athena is the lighter path. It would need a dedicated analytics bucket and KMS key rather than the images bucket, which already mixes images with code artifacts, and an IAM role scoped to that bucket. The export is charged for the whole cluster each run. m0022 m0027 shopnow-data-example00003-vxnr68dwirnv
  • A data lake, streaming ingestion, a governance layer or a BI rollout would have no consumer or freshness requirement to serve today; I would not raise them until the questions above have answers. shopnow-data-dbcluster-example00001
  • Running reports on a new Aurora reader is a third option once a reader exists, but readers share the cluster storage and the reader's first job is failover; mixing heavy analytical queries onto the failover target is worth avoiding. m0005

No change recommended in this area for now; the reasons are under "Not now".

Depends on other areas

  • Database Specialist SA Agent · A reader for failover, longer backup retention, DeletionProtection and a custom cluster parameter group (rds.force_ssl=1) belong to the database review. If zero-ETL is chosen later, the logical replication settings should go into that same custom parameter group so the writer reboots once.
  • Database Specialist SA Agent · Separating chatbot code and k8s manifests from the product images bucket (m0022) and narrowing the S3 gateway endpoint policy (m0027) stay with the domain of those resources; any future analytics bucket would rely on that separation.
  • DevOps Specialist SA Agent · If an integration or export job is added, alarms on integration lag and failed export tasks, and on writer CPU and write IOPS, belong to the alarm set.
References

  • Getting started with Aurora zero-ETL integrations
  • Exporting DB cluster data to Amazon S3

GenAI Specialist SA Agent Conditional

The shopnow-genai stack runs a LangChain product Q&A chatbot on one EC2 instance (i-0example00002) that calls Amazon Bedrock with a role allowed bedrock:* on every resource. Model invocation logging is off in us-east-1, the three guardrails in the account belong to other projects, and nothing in IAM forces a guardrail on each call, so prompts and answers leave no record and have no workload-specific filter. As the GenAI Specialist SA Agent I would raise the controls first: narrow model access, turn on invocation logging, add a shopnow guardrail enforced by IAM, and build a small evaluation set before any model or prompt change. Whether retrieval or any other AI service has a place depends on questions for the owner about what the chatbot answers and how much it is used.

What we see now

  • The shopnow-genai template describes the chatbot as a LangChain + Bedrock product Q&A service on one t3.large instance in shopnow-app-a, reachable only from the VPC on port 8000, with IMDSv2 required and an encrypted root volume. Those network and host settings already work well. s0020 i-0example00002 f0004
  • The instance role shopnow-genai-InstanceRole-VR63Qdfh4abE allows bedrock:* on *. The template comment says only InvokeModel on two models is needed; bedrock:* also allows creating agents, knowledge bases, custom models and provisioned throughput. m0002 s0127 s0020
  • Model invocation logging is not configured in us-east-1 (GetModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration returned no configuration), and the application log group /shopnow/ec2/chatbot has no log events and no retention, so there is no record of prompts, answers, token use or errors. f0068 s0078 f0086 f0034
  • Three guardrails exist in us-east-1 (otherapp-dev-retrieval-guardrail, otherapp-gw-dev-content-guard, otherapp-dev-guardrail), all as DRAFT versions and named for other projects. The chatbot role has no bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier condition, and the chatbot source was not available to show whether a guardrail is passed per call. f0069 s0079 e0169
  • The chatbot can read the Aurora master credential (shopnow/db) and objects under chatbot/ and seed/ in the images bucket, which suggests it answers from the catalog database; which tables or documents ground the answers is not visible in the evidence. s0127 m0013 shopnow-data-example00003-vxnr68dwirnv

Not now

  • Bedrock Knowledge Bases (retrieval): the chatbot appears to read the catalog database directly, and which data grounds its answers is unknown. Retrieval would be worth comparing only once the owner confirms that answers need documents (policies, manuals) that are not in the database and the evaluation set shows wrong or ungrounded answers. s0127 s0020
  • Bedrock Agents or AgentCore: the evidence shows a single question-and-answer flow, not tool selection or multi-step stateful work. A real workflow such as order lookup with per-user authorization would change this view. s0020
  • SageMaker AI, Trainium and Inferentia: there is no custom model, training data or self-hosted inference in scope; the chatbot uses managed Bedrock models. i-0example00002
  • Rekognition, Textract, Transcribe, Polly and Comprehend: no image-analysis, document, audio or text-classification workflow appears in the evidence. The images bucket holds product images, so image tagging could be something to explore with the owner, not a recommendation. shopnow-data-example00003-vxnr68dwirnv
  • AWS Security Agent and AWS DevOps Agent: alarms, logs and dashboards for the chatbot are not in place yet, so there is no operating data for an agent to work from; logging, alarms and runbooks come first. f0084 f0090 f0086
  • Changing the model: without usage, quality or cost data there is no basis to recommend another model; the evaluation set and invocation logs are the prerequisite. f0068

Recommendations

1. Narrow the chatbot's Bedrock permission to the models it calls Days of workCost neutral

What changes In stack shopnow-genai, resource InstanceRole, policy chatbot: replace Action bedrock:* on Resource * with bedrock:InvokeModel and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream (plus bedrock:ApplyGuardrail once a guardrail exists) on the foundation-model or inference-profile ARNs the chatbot uses.

What it gives A compromised or misconfigured chatbot host could then only call the models it needs, instead of creating agents, knowledge bases, custom models or provisioned throughput in the account.

Before deciding Confirm the two model IDs from the chatbot source or configuration, or from CloudTrail InvokeModel events for this role; IAM Access Analyzer policy generation could give a starting policy. Check whether the chatbot calls Converse or uses a cross-Region inference profile, because the profile and the underlying model ARNs then both need to be allowed.

Alternatives Keep bedrock:* for now and add an explicit Deny on the control-plane actions (CreateAgent, CreateKnowledgeBase, CreateModelCustomizationJob, CreateProvisionedModelThroughput) as an interim guard. Keep the current policy, since the account is non-production, and accept the risk until hosting moves.

How to undo Restore the previous chatbot policy document from the template history and update the stack.

Based on m0002 s0127 s0020

2. Turn on model invocation logging for us-east-1 with a retention period Setting changeMeasure first

What changes Configure Bedrock model invocation logging in us-east-1 to a dedicated CloudWatch Logs group (for example /shopnow/bedrock/invocations) with a retention period, text data delivery on, and read access limited to the operators who review it; S3 delivery is an option when long retention is needed.

What it gives Prompts, answers, token counts and errors become reviewable, which is the data needed to judge answer quality, cost and misuse and to build the evaluation set.

Before deciding Logging is an account and Region setting: confirm with the account owner, because other projects in this account (the otherapp-dev and otherapp-gw-dev guardrails suggest some) would be logged too. Agree what customer data may appear in prompts and how long it may be kept, and whether the log group needs a KMS key.

Alternatives Log prompts, answers and token use inside the chatbot to /shopnow/ec2/chatbot instead, with retention set; this covers only this workload but depends on the application code. Deliver to S3 with a lifecycle rule when retention is long and reads are rare.

How to undo Delete the model invocation logging configuration; the log group and its retention can stay or be deleted.

Based on f0068 s0078

3. Give the chatbot its own guardrail and enforce it in IAM Days of workMeasure first

What changes Create a shopnow product Q&A guardrail (content filters, denied topics outside the product catalog, PII masking for customer details), publish a numbered version, pass it on every chatbot call, and add the bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier condition with an explicit Deny for calls without it to the chatbot policy.

What it gives Every model call from the chatbot passes a filter defined for this use case, and a call without it is refused by IAM rather than relying on the code path.

Before deciding Ask the owner which topics the chatbot should refuse and whether customers can type personal data into it. Check in the chatbot source whether LangChain passes guardrail settings on the Bedrock call; the source was not part of this collection. Test the guardrail against sample questions from the evaluation set to see how often it blocks valid product questions.

Alternatives Reuse one of the existing guardrails after publishing a version, if its policies match the product Q&A use (they were created for other projects). Call ApplyGuardrail only on the user input first and add output checks later.

How to undo Remove the GuardrailIdentifier condition from the policy and the guardrail setting from the chatbot call; the guardrail version can stay unused.

Based on f0069 s0079 e0169 m0002

4. Build an evaluation set before changing the model or the prompt Weeks of workMeasure first

What changes Collect representative product questions with expected answers drawn from the catalog (from the owner and, once logging is on, from real traffic), and run them as a Bedrock model evaluation job or a scripted check whenever the model, prompt or LangChain version changes.

What it gives A model or prompt change can be compared against a known baseline for correctness, refusals and latency instead of being judged by impression.

Before deciding Who owns the chatbot's answers and can confirm expected answers? What counts as a correct answer: catalog facts only, or also recommendations and policies?

Alternatives A short manual checklist of questions reviewed by the owner before each change. Keep the current model and prompt unchanged until usage justifies an evaluation effort.

How to undo Stop running the evaluation; it does not change the running service.

Based on s0020 i-0example00002 f0068

Depends on other areas

  • Container & Serverless Specialist SA Agent · The chatbot is one t3.large instance in us-east-1a with no Auto Scaling group, load balancer or health replacement (m0020). Where it runs and how it survives an instance or AZ failure belongs to the Container & Serverless review; the GenAI controls here do not depend on the hosting choice, but the new role must carry the narrowed Bedrock policy and guardrail condition.
  • DevOps Specialist SA Agent · The chatbot is installed from chatbot/chatbot.tgz in the images bucket by UserData without a version (m0021, m0022); a pipeline and a dedicated artifact bucket belong to DevOps. Alarms and metrics for the chatbot host (f0084, f0090), the empty log group /shopnow/ec2/chatbot (f0086, f0034) and alarms on Bedrock throttling and errors once invocation logging is on belong to the alarm and log set.
  • Database Specialist SA Agent · The chatbot role can read the Aurora master credential shopnow/db (m0013) and reach Aurora through the app-subnet CIDR rule (m0014). A read-only database user for the chatbot belongs to the Database review; it also limits what a prompt-injected query could reach.

DevOps Specialist SA Agent Conditional

shopnow has one working pipeline: catalog-api goes from CodeCommit through CodeBuild to ECS and tags images with the commit, but it has no test or scan gate, and order-api, storefront and recommendation have no delivery path in the account. A bad release is not rolled back automatically, every repository allows tags to be overwritten, and the only alarm notifies an SNS topic with no subscriber. I would raise the alarm path first, because it is a cost-neutral setting, then cheap rollback, then pipeline gates and the telemetry the alarms need.

What we see now

  • The pipeline shopnow-catalog-api (CodePipeline V2) runs Source → Build → Deploy on every push to main through an EventBridge rule. Its run history shows one successful run, the initial import at commit 90e37b4d, and one failed run at creation, so it works but there is no delivery history to measure yet. s0061 s0062 s0063 shopnow-catalog-api
  • The buildspec builds and pushes the image with an 8-character commit tag and deploys that tag, which is good traceability; it also pushes latest, and has no test, scan or approval step. CodeBuild runs with privilegedMode=true for docker build, so any commit to main builds and reaches ECS unchecked. s0134 s0064 f0074 m0026
  • No pipeline was found for order-api, storefront or recommendation; their ECR repositories hold only a latest tag, and the order-api task definition uses order-api:latest. All four repositories are MUTABLE with scanOnPush=false, so a running task can be replaced by a different image and there is no earlier tag to roll back to. s0058 s0059 s0060 m0019 f0048 f0050 f0054 f0056 f0047
  • Both ECS services deploy with the circuit breaker off (enable=False, rollback=False), so a failed rollout keeps trying instead of returning to the last working revision. m0010 m0011 s0008
  • Operating feedback is thin: one alarm (catalog CPU) notifies shopnow-alerts, which has 0 subscriptions; the dashboard shopnow-overview has an ALB widget pointing at a placeholder load balancer; Container Insights is off on ECS, the EKS cluster has no observability add-on and no control plane logs, and the four log groups never expire. m0003 s0075 m0028 f0059 f0091 m0006 f0033
  • Infrastructure is mostly in CloudFormation (seven shopnow stacks; 73% of tagged resources in the Region carry stack tags), which gives a clean place for every change below; drift was not checked in this read-only assessment. f0106 f0121 f0123 f0125

Not now

  • OpenTelemetry/ADOT for distributed tracing: the evidence shows four services with no tracing need or latency problem across service boundaries. Worth revisiting when a request path across catalog-api, order-api and the EKS services needs to be followed end to end; CloudWatch Application Signals could be the first step then. f0059 f0091
  • Amazon Managed Grafana: one account, one workload and one dashboard; CloudWatch dashboards cover this. It would be worth considering if the team already uses Grafana or needs one view across several accounts or data sources. m0028
  • Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus: no Prometheus metrics or PromQL use is in the evidence, and the EKS workload definitions could not be read. Knowing whether storefront and recommendation export Prometheus metrics would decide it. m0030
  • Replacing CodePipeline, CodeBuild or CodeCommit: the pipeline works for catalog-api; extending it is the smaller change. A switch makes sense only if the organisation standardises on another CI system. s0063
  • A manual approval stage or a separate staging environment: the scope records this account as non-production, so automated test and health gates give most of the protection now. This changes when a production environment is added behind the same pipeline. f0074
  • Stack drift results are unknown for all seven stacks; the owner could run drift detection before the template changes above, since the pipeline already changes the catalog-api task definition outside CloudFormation. f0121 f0122 f0123 f0124 f0125 f0126 f0127
  • VPC Flow Logs on vpc-0example00001: useful for network troubleshooting and security review, but no network incident is in the evidence; worth adding with a retention period if the security review asks for it. f0107

Recommendations

1. Make the existing alarm reach a person, then add the alarm set each tier needs Days of workCost up

What changes In shopnow-observability, add an AWS::SNS::Subscription on shopnow-alerts for the team's on-call email or chat channel and send a test notification. Then add CloudWatch alarms in the stacks that own each resource: HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count, HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count, TargetResponseTime and UnHealthyHostCount for shopnow-internal and shopnow-eks-ingress; running task count for catalog-api and order-api; CPU, DatabaseConnections and FreeableMemory for the Aurora writer; StatusCheckFailed for the bastion and chatbot hosts. Replace the placeholder dimension in the shopnow-overview dashboard with the real load balancer and add one row per tier.

What it gives An alarm that fires today reaches nobody. With a subscriber and a small alarm set, a failed release, an unhealthy target or a database problem is seen by a person instead of by a customer, and the dashboard shows the components that actually run.

Before deciding Who owns this workload in operation and which channel should receive alarms (f0128)? Agree thresholds with the owners; for a non-production account, fewer alarms routed to a chat channel could be enough.

Alternatives Keep the single alarm and only add the subscription (the cost-neutral first step). Use CloudWatch Application Signals service-level objectives for the ECS APIs once Container Insights is on, instead of hand-built latency alarms.

How to undo Delete the subscription and the added alarms from the templates and update the stacks; the topic and the existing alarm stay as they are.

Based on m0003 f0076 f0077 f0078 f0079 f0081 f0083 f0084 m0028 shopnow-alerts

2. Make a bad ECS release cheap to undo Days of workCost neutral

What changes In shopnow-ecs, set DeploymentConfiguration.DeploymentCircuitBreaker {Enable: true, Rollback: true} on CatalogService and OrderService, and consider DeploymentConfiguration.Alarms with the target 5XX alarm from the first recommendation so a release that starts but fails under traffic also rolls back. Remove the 'docker push ...:latest' line from buildspec.yml, change the stack parameters CatalogImageTag and OrderImageTag from latest to a commit tag, rebuild order-api with a commit tag, and then set imageTagMutability=IMMUTABLE on all four shopnow ECR repositories.

What it gives A release whose tasks fail to start returns to the last COMPLETED deployment automatically, and every running task points at an image that cannot change under it, so a scaling or AZ event starts the same image and an earlier tag is always available to redeploy.

Before deciding Confirm how storefront and recommendation are pushed to ECR; immutability rejects a second push of latest, so every producer has to move to unique tags first. Note that the pipeline registers task definitions outside the template: a stack update with CatalogImageTag=latest would roll catalog-api back to latest, so the parameter needs the commit tag too. Health checks decide what 'failed' means: the shallow /catalog/health check (m0024) limits what the circuit breaker can detect.

Alternatives Keep MUTABLE repositories but deploy by image digest in the task definitions. Move catalog-api to an ECS blue/green deployment with CodeDeploy when a bake period with test traffic is wanted; more moving parts than the circuit breaker.

How to undo Set the circuit breaker back to disabled and the repositories back to MUTABLE in the templates; images already pushed keep their tags.

Based on m0010 m0011 m0019 f0048 f0050 f0054 f0056 s0134 catalog-api order-api order-api storefront catalog-api recommendation

3. Add test and scan gates to the catalog-api pipeline, then reuse it for order-api Weeks of workCost up

What changes Add a Test stage to shopnow-catalog-api between Build and Deploy (or test commands in the existing buildspec) that runs the unit tests and publishes them to a CodeBuild report group, and fail the build when they fail. Turn on scanOnPush (or Amazon Inspector enhanced scanning for the registry) and fail the stage when findings above an agreed severity are present. Then copy the shopnow-cicd pattern for order-api so it is built from source with a commit tag instead of pushed by hand.

What it gives A change that breaks tests or ships a known vulnerable package stops before it reaches the ECS service, and order-api gets the same traceability catalog-api already has: which commit runs where.

Before deciding catalog-api has no test files in the repository today (Dockerfile, app.py, buildspec.yml, requirements.txt only); the tests have to be written first. Where is the order-api, storefront and recommendation source kept, and does the team use another CI system? If so, the same gates belong there instead. Agree the severity threshold for scan findings and who triages them.

Alternatives Keep the pipeline as it is and only turn on registry scanning with findings reviewed after the fact. Run the same test and scan gates in the team's existing CI system (for example GitHub Actions) and keep CodePipeline only for the ECS deploy.

How to undo Remove the Test stage and the scan settings from shopnow-cicd and the ECR templates; the pipeline returns to Source → Build → Deploy.

Based on f0074 m0026 f0047 f0049 f0053 f0055 s0061 s0131 shopnow-catalog-api shopnow-catalog-api 00000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000003

4. Give the alarms something to watch: container metrics, cluster logs and log retention Days of workMeasure first

What changes Set containerInsights to enhanced on the ECS cluster shopnow; install the amazon-cloudwatch-observability add-on on the EKS cluster shopnow (the add-on can use the existing EKS Pod Identity agent); enable the audit and authenticator control plane log types; set RetentionInDays on /shopnow/ecs/catalog-api, /shopnow/ecs/order-api, /shopnow/ec2/chatbot and /shopnow/codebuild; and find out why /shopnow/ecs/order-api has had no events for 9 days and /shopnow/ec2/chatbot has none.

What it gives Task restarts, memory, pod and node health become visible and alarmable, cluster access is recorded, log storage stops growing without limit, and a silent log group stops hiding a failed service.

Before deciding Agree a retention period per log group with the owner (compliance requirements are unknown). Container Insights and control plane logs are charged by ingested data; measure the volume for a short period on this non-production account before turning everything on.

Alternatives Turn on only ECS Container Insights in standard mode and the EKS audit log, and keep the rest as today. Use a Fluent Bit or Prometheus collector the team already runs, if there is one, instead of the add-on.

How to undo Set containerInsights back to disabled, remove the add-on and the log types, and remove RetentionInDays; logs already expired cannot be restored.

Seven directions at a glance

DirectionStatusReviewed byReason
ContainersConditionalContainer & Serverless Specialist SA AgentECS Fargate already runs catalog-api and order-api across two AZs. Packaging the chatbot there fixes its single point of failure and gives it versioned images; consolidating storefront and recommendation onto the same platform is worth deciding once their Kubernetes manifests have been read (m0030).
ServerlessNot recommendedContainer & Serverless Specialist SA AgentNo event or request unit in the evidence that fits Lambda better than the current containers.
Managed databaseConditionalDatabase Specialist SA AgentKeep Aurora PostgreSQL and ElastiCache, which are already managed services, and raise their configuration: free recovery settings first, then per-service credentials and required TLS, then paid failover targets when recovery goals are agreed. No evidence supports changing the engine.
Managed analyticsNot assessedData Analytics Specialist SA AgentTemplates and source show order and product data in Aurora PostgreSQL shopnow with one writer and no reader. No shopnow stack declares analytics services; the Athena workgroups and OpenSearch spend belong to other workloads. Demand is unknown, so the pathway is not assessed rather than scored low.
Generative AIConditionalGenAI Specialist SA AgentKeep Amazon Bedrock for the existing chatbot and add controls: least-privilege model access, model invocation logging, a workload guardrail enforced through bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier, and an evaluation set. Usage, owner and grounding data are unknown, so the pathway stays conditional; no new AI service is proposed.
Cloud-native structureConditionalContainer & Serverless Specialist SA AgentImprovements within the current service structure: Application Auto Scaling on CPU, a readiness check against Aurora, HTTPS listeners and header validation. No messaging product is selected because no asynchronous step is in the evidence.
Modern DevOpsConditionalDevOps Specialist SA AgentThe pipeline pattern, commit tagging and CloudFormation coverage already exist, so the smallest changes extend them: an alarm path that reaches a person, circuit breakers and immutable tags, test and scan gates, and container telemetry. Business goals, operating ownership and delivery metrics are not in the evidence, so the pathway stays conditional.

Recommended = the evidence supports it now; Recommended when conditions are met = worth doing once the conditions hold; Not recommended = the evidence argues against it today; Not assessed = the evidence needed to judge it is missing. The order of work is left to the conversation with the workload owner.

Amazon EKS Auto Mode
Containers
EKS Auto Mode automates compute autoscaling (creates nodes when pods do not fit, removes low-utilization nodes), networking (load balancers for Service and Ingress) and block storage for an EKS cluster; Karpenter, VPC CNI, CoreDNS and the AWS Load Balancer Controller are installed and updated by AWS.Managed node provisioning and scaling for an existing EKS cluster; removes fixed node groups and right-sizing work.

Terms used in this report

TermMeaning
RTORecovery time objective: how long the service may be down after a failure before it hurts the business.
RPORecovery point objective: how much recent data the business can afford to lose after a failure.
Multi-AZRunning copies in two or more Availability Zones (separate data centres in one region) so one zone's failure does not stop the service.
IaCInfrastructure as code: templates (CloudFormation, CDK, Terraform) that create the resources, so changes are reviewed like code.
driftA difference between a stack's template and the resources as they are now, usually from a change made outside the template.
DeletionPolicyA CloudFormation setting that decides what happens to a resource when its stack is deleted: delete it, keep it, or snapshot it first.
IMDSv2The session-based version of the EC2 instance metadata service, which blocks a common way of stealing instance credentials.
least privilegeGiving a role only the actions and resources it actually uses.
circuit breakerAn ECS deployment setting that stops a failing deployment and rolls back to the last working version automatically.
PodDisruptionBudgetA Kubernetes rule that keeps a minimum number of pods running while nodes are drained or upgraded.
HPAHorizontal Pod Autoscaler: Kubernetes adds or removes pods based on load.
KarpenterAn open-source node autoscaler for Kubernetes that starts right-sized nodes when pods need them.
EKS Auto ModeAn EKS mode in which AWS runs the worker nodes, their scaling and their upgrades for the cluster.
RDS ProxyA managed connection pool in front of RDS and Aurora that lets many application instances share a few database connections.
SpotSpare EC2 capacity at a lower price that AWS can take back with two minutes' notice; suited to work that can restart.
zero-ETLAn AWS integration that copies operational data into an analytics service continuously without a pipeline the team has to run.
GravitonAWS-designed Arm processors; the same workload usually costs less per unit of performance on them.
Savings PlansA one- or three-year spend commitment that lowers the hourly price of compute.
guardrailIn Amazon Bedrock, a policy that filters harmful or off-topic prompts and answers.
Pod IdentityAn EKS feature that gives each pod its own IAM role instead of sharing the node's role.
extended supportPaid support for a Kubernetes or database version after standard support ends; billed per hour on top of the normal price.
Performance InsightsAn RDS and Aurora feature that shows which queries and waits use the database's capacity.
Container InsightsCloudWatch metrics and logs for ECS and EKS clusters, services and tasks.
Specialist SA AgentAn AI agent that takes the role of an AWS specialist solutions architect for one technology area (containers, databases, analytics, generative AI, DevOps); its advice is a draft the assessing architect confirms.

Evidence

Reference codes: f0001 = a finding from an automated check (f, then its number); m0001 = a finding written during the assessment from templates, policies and source code; e0001 = the inventory API call it rests on; s0001 = supplementary evidence (stack templates, IAM policies, task definitions, source files); h0001 = host inspection; p001 = a published list price. Method and provenance

How the grades are derived
GradeMeaningRule (first match wins)
Fix firstAt least one high-severity item to fix. Worth settling before any modernization step.one or more FAIL with HIGH severity
Needs workFailures or several warnings. Worth planning in the first wave.any FAIL, or 3+ WARN
WatchMinor warnings, or open questions the configuration cannot answer. Confirm with evidence before relying on it.1-2 WARN, or any open question (UNKNOWN)
SoundEvery judged check passed and no question is open. Keep as is and re-check on change.all judged checks PASS and no open question
UnassessedNo judged evidence yet.no judged or unknown checks

Grades are derived only from the judged checks listed in this report; every grade can be traced to the findings that produced it. They are not AWS Well-Architected Tool ratings. The numeric local score (PASS 1 · WARN 0.5 · FAIL 0, weighted) remains in the method appendix for pathway ranking.

Numeric scores (for pathway ranking)

Local score = weighted average of PASS 1, WARN 0.5, FAIL 0 over judged checks; UNKNOWN is excluded and only lowers evidence coverage. These are inputs to pathway ranking, not a rating of the workload.
